{"id": "79:23/q02", "question": "Whom did Pharaoh gather?", "turns_on": "Which episode this brief gathering recalls: a public proclamation, the contest with Moses, protection from the serpent, or pursuit of the Israelites; the use of 26:53 and 20:60 to identify this gathering is specifically disputed.", "positions": [{"id": "79:23/q02/p1", "position": "His people or subjects, sometimes specified as Copts, inhabitants of his kingdom, or people together with soldiers.", "reasons": "Muqātil specifies Copts; al-Ṭabarī says people and followers and reports Ibn Zayd's account of their assembling before the proclamation. Al-Naḥḥās cites Ibn Zayd for the understood object. Al-Māwardī and al-Qurṭubī say they were gathered to attend. Al-Wāḥidī's Basīṭ, al-Baghawī, al-Ṭabrisī, and Ibn al-Jawzī specify people and soldiers or troops; Ibn ʿAṭiyya says people of his kingdom. Ibn ʿĀshūr specifies city inhabitants of every class. Al-Ālūsī also reports subjects as an alternative to troops. Study Quran attributes assembly of people for the sovereignty declaration to most commentators."}, {"id": "79:23/q02/p2", "position": "The magicians gathered for their contest or plot.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī links the gathering to al-Shuʿarāʾ (26:53). Bursawī says Pharaoh assembled the sorcerers and their devices and links this to 20:60. Al-Ālūsī calls this the most supported explanation, citing the sending of summoners (26:53) and assembly of plotters (20:60). Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī reports the same citations but argues that those passages do not establish that this gathering is the same event."}, {"id": "79:23/q02/p3", "position": "The magicians together with soldiers, officials, or an army.", "reasons": "Al-Māwardī says the magicians were assembled for a contest and the army summoned to fight. Al-Qurṭubī likewise assigns the soldiers to battle and sorcerers to Moses' challenge. Al-Nasafī names magicians and troops; al-Biqāʿī says Pharaoh gathered magicians by choice or force and added soldiers; Abū Ḥayyān names magicians and officials."}, {"id": "79:23/q02/p4", "position": "The magicians together with his people.", "reasons": "Al-Wāḥidī's Wajīz explicitly names both groups."}, {"id": "79:23/q02/p5", "position": "His troops or army and elite.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī reports the troops as one alternative. Elmalılı places the collection of the army and elite after the magicians' defeat, with collectors sent through the cities, and cites al-Shuʿarāʾ (26:53)."}, {"id": "79:23/q02/p6", "position": "His companions, for protection against the serpent.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī reports this motive; it corresponds to the account of Pharaoh fleeing the serpent in fear."}, {"id": "79:23/q02/p7", "position": "His people summoned to pursue the Israelites.", "reasons": "Study Quran reports this as an alternative connected to 26:53."}]}
{"id": "79:23/q03", "question": "Why are the verbs' objects left unstated?", "turns_on": "Whether context supplies the omitted people, only the actions matter, or the sense of ḥashara itself supplies a crowd.", "positions": [{"id": "79:23/q03/p1", "position": "The objects are understood from context: he gathered his people and called to them.", "reasons": "Al-Naḥḥās cites Ibn Zayd for the omitted object of ḥashara. Al-Samīn says both verbs omit their objects but can be supplied as people and the call to them. Ibn ʿĀshūr says the obvious object of ḥashara is the city's inhabitants from every class."}, {"id": "79:23/q03/p2", "position": "The objects are omitted because the actions themselves are the point.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn gives this as the other explanation of both omissions."}, {"id": "79:23/q03/p3", "position": "Ḥashara itself clearly implies a crowd, so no object needs stating.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shāṭiʾ bases this on the word's explicit sense of assembling a crowd."}]}
{"id": "79:23/q04", "question": "In what order did the gathering and call occur?", "turns_on": "Whether the two verbs give the event's actual chronology or a sequence whose real order Ibn ʿAbbās reverses.", "positions": [{"id": "79:23/q04/p1", "position": "He gathered the people and then called out to them.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī reports Ibn Zayd's sequence: the crowd assembled, Pharaoh declared himself their highest lord, then God punished him in both lives (79:24–25). Al-Māwardī says the people attended before he addressed them. Ibn al-Jawzī explicitly puts the call after their assembly; al-Nasafī and Abū Ḥayyān locate the call at the assembly."}, {"id": "79:23/q04/p2", "position": "He called first, then gathered the people, despite the verse's wording order.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya reports this explanation from Ibn ʿAbbās."}]}
{"id": "79:23/q05", "question": "How and through whom did Pharaoh call out?", "turns_on": "Whether Pharaoh personally voiced the proclamation or a herald voiced it for him; Bint al-Shāṭiʾ disputes textual support for the herald.", "positions": [{"id": "79:23/q05/p1", "position": "He addressed the assembled people himself.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī, Bursawī, and al-Ālūsī allow a personal address alongside a herald. Al-Nasafī places the call where those assembled met; Abū Ḥayyān says he addressed that assembly. Al-Qurṭubī adds that the call was loud. Ibn Kathīr locates the call among his people."}, {"id": "79:23/q05/p2", "position": "A herald announced Pharaoh's words on his behalf.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī, Bursawī, and al-Ālūsī give this as an alternative; al-Biqāʿī says the herald's words represented Pharaoh's own. Bint al-Shāṭiʾ rejects al-Zamakhsharī's suggestion that Pharaoh ordered a caller to announce his message because she says the text does not support it."}, {"id": "79:23/q05/p3", "position": "He called loudly.", "reasons": "Al-Qurṭubī explicitly explains the call as a loud voice."}]}
{"id": "79:23/q06", "question": "What did Pharaoh proclaim?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "79:23/q06/p1", "position": "He claimed to be his people's highest lord.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabarī calls the claim a foolish lie and reports Ibn Zayd's account that God then seized Pharaoh in punishment for both lives (79:24–25). Ibn ʿAṭiyya also states the claim. Al-Rāzī places it at the gathering. Al-Samīn says the following fa-qāla explains the content of the call. Study Quran describes the announcement as a declaration of sovereignty."}]}
{"id": "79:23/q07", "question": "How does his prior turning away and striving lead into this gathering?", "turns_on": "The preceding adbara and yasʿā may describe flight, scheming, the start of action, figurative rejection, literal angry departure, or an evasive pretext; al-Ālūsī tests the flight account against thumma and the timing of the magicians' gathering.", "positions": [{"id": "79:23/q07/p1", "position": "He fled the serpent in fright, then sought protection or acted rashly.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī reports fear after seeing the serpent and al-Ḥasan's description of Pharaoh as reckless and quick-moving; Bursawī transmits al-Kashshāf's terrified flight and al-Ḥasan's rash, impulsive Pharaoh. Al-Qurṭubī reports gathering companions for protection. Al-Ālūsī objects that flight fits poorly after the customary gathering of magicians and, if earlier, leaves the delay indicated by thumma unclear; he also allows that the wording might emphasize the shock of the flight."}, {"id": "79:23/q07/p2", "position": "He turned from Moses and exerted himself to plot against him, including mustering magicians.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī reports this reading. Al-Biqāʿī says the turning led him to gather magicians voluntarily or by force and add soldiers. Ibn ʿĀshūr reads the striving figuratively as strenuous efforts to prevent people hearing Moses and to gather magicians against what Pharaoh mistook for sorcery, citing 20:60. Bursawī says the effort came from obstinacy, not confidence that the sign could really be matched."}, {"id": "79:23/q07/p3", "position": "Adbara means he began to act or proceed, with a hint of ruin.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī compares adbara to aqbala yafʿalu and says adbara avoids describing Pharaoh as approaching. Al-Ālūsī allows an ironic use of 'began' that signals his ruin."}, {"id": "79:23/q07/p4", "position": "Turning away figuratively means rejecting the invitation to faith.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr compares Musaylima's rejection and quotes the Prophet's warning that God would have Musaylima killed if he turned away."}, {"id": "79:23/q07/p5", "position": "He literally left in anger and moved quickly.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr allows this reading of both preceding verbs as an angry, rejecting departure. Bursawī cites al-Rāghib's gloss of adbara as presenting one's back and explains 'striving' grammatically as a circumstantial qualifier of the subject, meaning he hurried and exerted himself."}, {"id": "79:23/q07/p6", "position": "His effort was a pretext to avoid the gathering or court.", "reasons": "Bursawī calls it a false pretext."}]}
{"id": "79:23/q08", "question": "What does this action show about human agency?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "79:23/q08/p1", "position": "Human acts originate with the servants themselves.", "reasons": "Jishumi cites Pharaoh's transgression, denial, turning away, and calling out as evidence."}]}
{"id": "79:23/q09", "question": "How does gathering here relate to the sūra's theme?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "79:23/q09/p1", "position": "It echoes the final gathering and the sūra's establishment of resurrection and humanity's fate.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī says the sūra establishes resurrection and the gathering, displays humanity's final fate after the preceding sūras' exposition, and uses oaths to mark the decisive climax. Jishumi connects ḥashr with the Day of Gathering; Bint al-Shāṭiʾ says the Qurʾan uses the word most often for the Last Day, in more than thirty places."}]}

{"id": "79:24/q01", "question": "What does the initial فاء convey?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "79:24/q01/p1", "position": "Pharaoh spoke as soon as the people arrived, eager to make the proclamation.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr reads the فاء as marking this immediate succession."}]}
{"id": "79:24/q02", "question": "How does 'he said' relate to the preceding call or striving?", "turns_on": "Whether the statement explicates the call, coordinates with the earlier action, or requires an implied speech verb.", "positions": [{"id": "79:24/q02/p1", "position": "It restates the preceding call, with the repeated conjunction emphasizing the apposition.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr compares the repeated conjunction in 6:99."}, {"id": "79:24/q02/p2", "position": "It is coordinated with 'he strove,' so the proclamation was ordered throughout the kingdom.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr offers this alternative, extending the speech beyond the crowd by the palace."}, {"id": "79:24/q02/p3", "position": "An implied 'he says' introduces the quoted claim.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī says this second parsing requires an additional figurative use."}]}
{"id": "79:24/q03", "question": "How was Pharaoh's claim delivered and to whom?", "turns_on": "Whether Pharaoh spoke to the gathered people himself or had the claim announced for him.", "positions": [{"id": "79:24/q03/p1", "position": "He addressed the assembled people himself.", "reasons": "Muqātil in al-Wāḥidī places him on his throne; Ibn ʿAṭiyya has him gather the kingdom; al-Ālūsī and Elmalılı describe an assembled audience and a ruler's speech. Al-Rāzī allows a personal address at the magicians' gathering, linked to 26:53. Kuran Yolu says he assembled magicians and men. Ibn ʿĀshūr notes that followers and soldiers could have carried out the gathering and call by his command, as al-Manṣūr is said to have built Baghdad. Ibn ʿĀshūr also says the object of 'called' is omitted, and explains that calling literally summons by raised voice or can mean merely raising the voice; he cites al-Ḥarīrī's thirtieth Maqāma and the accusative after vocative particles."}, {"id": "79:24/q03/p2", "position": "He had an announcer deliver the claim, or ordered its proclamation beyond the gathered crowd.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī gives an announcer as an alternative to Pharaoh speaking personally; Ibn ʿĀshūr's coordinated construction makes it an order throughout the kingdom."}]}
{"id": "79:24/q04", "question": "Did he call before or after gathering the people?", "turns_on": "Whether the sequence of calling and gathering is read in the order narrated or reversed.", "positions": [{"id": "79:24/q04/p1", "position": "He proclaimed the claim after they gathered.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr reads the فاء as immediate proclamation on their arrival; al-Rāzī places the claim at the magicians' gathering."}, {"id": "79:24/q04/p2", "position": "He called first and then gathered the people.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya attributes this reading of the sequence to Ibn ʿAbbās."}]}
{"id": "79:24/q05", "question": "How long or elaborate was the proclamation?", "turns_on": "Whether the three-word quotation represents the whole utterance or a compressed extract of the speech in 43:51–55.", "positions": [{"id": "79:24/q05/p1", "position": "It was a terse three-word utterance, expressing the tyrant's alarm rather than a formal address.", "reasons": "Bint al-Shāṭiʾ connects its brevity with the sūra's decisive pace."}, {"id": "79:24/q05/p2", "position": "It belonged to a fuller speech boasting of Egypt's power and belittling Moses.", "reasons": "Iṣlāḥī draws the expanded speech from 43:51–55: Pharaoh boasts of Egypt's kingdom and rivers, disparages Moses, asks why he has no gold ornaments or angelic escort, and fools his disobedient people before their drowning."}]}
{"id": "79:24/q06", "question": "What force does 'I am your lord' have against Moses' call?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "79:24/q06/p1", "position": "Its restrictive form counters Moses' summons.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr identifies the restrictive wording as a response to Moses."}]}
{"id": "79:24/q07", "question": "What lordship did Pharaoh claim by 'your highest lord'?", "turns_on": "What Pharaoh counted as a 'lord': supreme deity, other gods or idols, human authorities, benefactor, proximate deity, inherited divine status, or apportioned divine nature.", "positions": [{"id": "79:24/q07/p1", "position": "He claimed supreme lordship, with no lord above him.", "reasons": "Muqātil, al-Wāḥidī, al-Baghawī, al-Ṭabrisī, Ibn al-Jawzī, al-Qurṭubī, al-Nasafī, Bursawī and Elmalılı give the no-higher-lord sense. Elmalılı adds that Pharaoh demanded worship, and reads his tower inquiry in 28:38 as tacit admission of a god whom he refused to rank above himself. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī says the wording and 28:38 and 26:29 support actual divinity rather than mere kingship."}, {"id": "79:24/q07/p2", "position": "He ranked himself above the gods or idols his people acknowledged.", "reasons": "ʿAṭāʾ says he made little idols for the people, told them to worship them, and claimed lordship of idols and worshipers; al-Baghawī, al-Ṭabrisī, Ibn al-Jawzī and al-Qurṭubī transmit this interpretation. Al-Kāshifī calls the idols likenesses of Pharaoh; al-Nasafī notes that the people did worship idols. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī regards this as the apparent sense among polytheists. Ibn ʿĀshūr offers the idea that Pharaoh was regarded as lord of many gods, making 'highest' explanatory. Al-Burhān reconciles 7:127 by saying the gods were his property and he first worshiped them in the people's religion before demanding the top rank."}, {"id": "79:24/q07/p3", "position": "He claimed supremacy over other human lords, leaders, kings, and officials.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzī and al-Qurṭubī report a hierarchy of chiefs over lower people; al-Bayḍāwī speaks of everyone managing people's affairs, and Bursawī of kings and officials. Al-Biqāʿī portrays humans as ranked lords with Pharaoh highest. Al-Ālūsī describes a speech elevating him above administrators. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī reports a political reading like Pharaoh's boast of Egypt's kingdom in 43:51, but rejects it as conflicting with the apparent wording and 28:38 and 26:29."}, {"id": "79:24/q07/p4", "position": "He meant that he alone nurtured, benefited, commanded and forbade his people, while denying a Creator and resurrection.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī and Bursawī portray Pharaoh as a materialist. For al-Rāzī, ربكم refers to nurturer and benefactor, since Pharaoh denied a deity and messenger. Both deny that he claimed to have created the cosmos: that would be self-evidently false, and a person insane enough to doubt a Creator could not have been sent a prophet."}, {"id": "79:24/q07/p5", "position": "He claimed to be the deity closest to people, administering their provisions, affairs and honor, unlike other gods.", "reasons": "Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī offers this possible meaning and cites 7:127."}, {"id": "79:24/q07/p6", "position": "He claimed the status of Amun-Ra's son and successor.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr offers this alternative, explaining that Egyptian priests called the king Amun-Ra's son and held the sun to be that god's manifestation."}, {"id": "79:24/q07/p7", "position": "He assumed divinity was a nature distributed among beings and that its highest possessor could best obtain what he wanted.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī identifies this as Pharaoh's premise behind ranking lords."}]}
{"id": "79:24/q08", "question": "Is 'highest' an absolute title or a comparison?", "turns_on": "Whether the superlative expresses an unrestricted title or a rank over other beings.", "positions": [{"id": "79:24/q08/p1", "position": "It is an absolute, unrestricted superlative, not 'higher than another.'", "reasons": "Bint al-Shāṭiʾ compares the form with superlatives in 92:15, 92:17 and 92:20."}, {"id": "79:24/q08/p2", "position": "It ranks Pharaoh above other lords, gods, or rulers.", "reasons": "Elmalılı explicitly says 'highest among lords'; al-Biqāʿī ranks humans as lords; Bursawī offers rank over subordinate kings; al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī reads superiority over acknowledged gods. Ibn ʿĀshūr says lordship over many gods could make 'highest' an explanatory epithet."}]}
{"id": "79:24/q09", "question": "Did Pharaoh claim to create the cosmos?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "79:24/q09/p1", "position": "No; a literal creator claim would be self-evidently false and irrational.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī and Bursawī say Pharaoh could not have meant that he created the heavens, earth, mountains, plants and animals; someone doubting the existence of a Creator would be insane, and God would not send a messenger to an insane person."}]}
{"id": "79:24/q10", "question": "How did belief in other gods coexist with Pharaoh's claim?", "turns_on": "Whether other gods were subordinate objects of worship, an implicitly admitted deity, or excluded by Pharaoh's materialism.", "positions": [{"id": "79:24/q10/p1", "position": "Other gods or idols existed in the people's religion, but Pharaoh claimed authority or the highest rank over them.", "reasons": "Al-Nasafī notes their idol worship. Al-Burhān says they were Pharaoh's property and he worshiped them before demanding the highest rank, reconciling 7:127. Al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī reads acknowledged polytheist gods; Ibn ʿĀshūr says the king was held to be lord of many gods."}, {"id": "79:24/q10/p2", "position": "Pharaoh's tower inquiry tacitly conceded a god, while he still denied that god stood above him.", "reasons": "Elmalılı connects this to Pharaoh's order to Hāmān in 28:38."}, {"id": "79:24/q10/p3", "position": "He denied any Creator while claiming practical control of his people.", "reasons": "Al-Rāzī and Bursawī describe him as a materialist denying Creator and resurrection."}]}

ow did this claim follow Pharaoh's earlier claim in 28:38?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "79:24/q11/p1", "position": "He first said he knew no god for his people besides himself, then later claimed to be their highest lord.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās and Mujāhid link both claims to God's seizure of Pharaoh. {"id": "79:24/q12", "question": "What did Moses offer Pharaoh before the boast, and how did Pharaoh respond?", "turns_on": "The reports differ on the promised duration and details of Pharaoh's response.", "positions": [{"id": "79:24/q12/p1", "position": "Moses offered lasting youth, kingship and Paradise for faith; Pharaoh refused, with Haman dissuading him in one report.", "reasons": "Muqātil says Moses offered continued kingship, youth without aging and Paradise if Pharaoh confessed God as Lord and himself as servant; Pharaoh retorted that a man is worshiped as lord only if he has a lord. {"id": "79:24/q13", "question": "Why did the boast seem incongruous after Moses' sign?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "79:24/q13/p1", "position": "The transformed staff had exposed Pharaoh's helplessness, making the claim sound deranged or uncomprehending.", "reasons": "Al-Qāḍī as cited by al-Rāzī and an unnamed view in Bursawī both draw this inference from his humiliation before the staff."}]}
{"id": "79:24/q14", "question": "What does the comparison with Moses' victory over magic show?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "79:24/q14/p1", "position": "Moses was the higher one after the magicians' defeat, because defeating their magic defeated Pharaoh.", "reasons": "Bursawī connects the claim with Moses' assurance in 20:68."}]}
{"id": "79:24/q15", "question": "What do the reports say Iblis made of Pharaoh's boast?", "turns_on": "The reports differ between Iblis's reflection on his own pride and a direct encounter with Pharaoh.", "positions": [{"id": "79:24/q15/p1", "position": "Iblis wondered what would befall Pharaoh for claiming lordship when his own pride had already brought disaster.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī transmits Satan's comparison with his offense against Adam; al-Qushayrī as reported by Bursawī says Iblīs had only claimed good for himself and suffered calamity."}, {"id": "79:24/q15/p2", "position": "Iblis confronted Pharaoh in an Egyptian bath and repeated the boast after Pharaoh failed to recognize his supposed creator.", "reasons": "Al-Thaʿlabī's account, reported by al-Qurṭubī, has Iblis appear as a man and challenge Pharaoh's failure to know one he claimed to have made."}]}
{"id": "79:24/q16", "question": "What does the verse show about the danger of royal deification?", "turns_on": "Whether the note states a general continuity or identifies a later dynasty and endpoint.", "positions": [{"id": "79:24/q16/p1", "position": "Pharaoh's fabrication persisted among Egypt's kings and followers.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAṭiyya calls it extreme fabrication; Abū Ḥayyān reports this assessment from him."}, {"id": "79:24/q16/p2", "position": "Egyptian royal deification later appeared under Ismaili rulers, from al-Muʿizz until Ṣalāḥ al-Dīn removed it.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān supplies this specific historical attribution."}]}
{"id": "79:24/q17", "question": "What inward impulse does Pharaoh's claim reveal?", "turns_on": "Whether the inward lesson centers on a universal impulse, its cure, or Pharaoh's spiritual expulsion.", "positions": [{"id": "79:24/q17/p1", "position": "An impulse toward lordship and mastery exists in every soul, though only some openly voice it.", "reasons": "Al-Ghazālī in al-Biqāʿī says the soul recoils from servitude; a gnostic says all souls harbor Pharaoh's claim and resentment at servants or subordinates reveals it. Al-Biqāʿī cites the Prophet's never reproaching a servant. Kuran Yolu's Ghazālī calls it a distorted desire for perfection, elevation and freedom, revealed by some and restrained by others; its authors cite ambition for rank and self-assertion."}, {"id": "79:24/q17/p2", "position": "True perfection and freedom come through knowing and obeying God; rival claims to selfhood bring decline.", "reasons": "Ghazālī as reported by Kuran Yolu adds turning to God, following His will and adopting divine character; he calls other self-claims misery."}, {"id": "79:24/q17/p3", "position": "Pharaoh's satanic schemes increased his veil, expelled him from the holy presence and led to subjugation and Fire.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī says the claim contested divine majesty, connecting its outcome to 79:25 and to anyone contesting God's grandeur and pride."}]}
{"id": "79:24/q18", "question": "Whom does al-Biqāʿī associate with Pharaoh's error?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "79:24/q18/p1", "position": "He associates Ibn ʿArabī, Ibn al-Fāriḍ, their followers and al-Ḥallāj with denial of the sovereign God.", "reasons": "Al-Biqāʿī curses the first group and places al-Ḥallāj after Pharaoh in that error."}]}
{"id": "79:24/q19", "question": "What does Pharaoh's boast show about divine power and the gravity of his sin?", "turns_on": "Whether the note stresses culpability and punishment or specifically refutes an asserted divine power.", "positions": [{"id": "79:24/q19/p1", "position": "It is a grave claim to divinity for which Pharaoh was seized and punished.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿAbbās and Mujāhid say God seized him for both divinity claims. Al-Qāshānī says contesting divine majesty brought subjugation and Fire (79:25). Asad calls claimed divine status Pharaoh's cardinal sin and transgression of right, cross-referencing 28:38 and 79:17.
